title: How people are using AI to cancel subscriptions, claim refunds
summary: CBS MoneyWatch reporter Megan Cerullo looks at consumers who hand chores like returns, refund claims, subscription cancellations and utility appointments to AI agents, with users describing recovered money and hours saved. Stanford economist Neale Mahoney argues that agents erode the hassle that companies quietly profit from, a cost one think tank puts at around $165 billion a year, which is why some large firms are already blocking agents from transacting. The founder of the agent's maker says the service still keeps a human on standby, while Groundwork Collaborative's Lindsay Owens warns that agents could end up nudging users toward products that earn their makers commissions.
focus: Shadow the stretch where the economist explains why companies have an incentive to block agents, then the closing warning about agents steering shoppers toward commission-paying products; both are compact, argument-driven passages with clear stress patterns.

vocab.meaning: available to be contacted and help at short notice
vocab.context: The founder said a person remains on standby in case the automated service gets stuck.

phrases.meaning: the money and time consumers lose to hassles, hidden fees and hard-to-cancel services that companies profit from
phrases.zh: “麻烦经济”（企业靠消费者的麻烦与隐性收费获利）
phrases.context: It was the story's central term for the profitable friction that AI agents are starting to undo.
phrases.example: Part of the subscription business's margin is really the annoyance economy, and that revenue is at risk once agents cancel on customers' behalf.

phrases.meaning: to refuse to accept bad treatment without fighting back

phrases.context: It described companies pushing back against agents, for instance by banning them from transactions.
phrases.example: The incumbent won't take the price war lying down, so our base case should assume a matching discount.

phrases.context: It described an agent scanning a user's inbox for refunds and money owed.
phrases.example: Legal will comb through the target's supplier contracts for change-of-control clauses before signing.

phrases.meaning: to treat a worry or problem as unimportant
phrases.context: It described consumers setting aside their fears about AI because the time and money savings are tangible.
phrases.example: Investors shrugged off the weak quarter because the order backlog kept growing.
